title: Money and paperwork
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: min faḍlika, hal yumkinu an + V

rules.text: A sign is written in the PASSIVE PARTICIPLE, and that is what this module teaches instead of the passive verb: maṭlūb (required), mamnūʿ (forbidden), maftūḥ (open), mughlaq (closed) — and L2-M7's mawjūd (present, in stock) turns out to have been one all along. They behave as ordinary adjectives and agree like ordinary adjectives: al-istimāra maṭlūba. The passive VERB (yuktabu, yudfaʿu) is L4's and is not opened here.

mamnūʿ takes a MAṢDAR after it — L3-M1's grammar, printed on a public notice: mamnūʿ at-tadkhīn, "smoking forbidden". Once you see that the -ing noun on the sign is the same word you met in "after work", half the signs in an Arab city stop being decoration.

The participle agrees with what it describes, and English participles never do: al-maktab maftūḥ but al-fātūra maṭlūba, at-tawqīʿ maṭlūb but al-istimāra maṭlūba. On a real sign you will see both endings within a metre of each other.

This module speaks the careful register throughout, and opens no new politeness shape to do it: min faḍlika is L1-M8's, law samaḥt is L2-M1's, hal yumkinu an is L3-M2's. A counter is exactly the place that decision was made for.

Numbers past L1-M8's range come in as VOCABULARY, not as a system: alf is a thousand, alfayn two thousand. A rent is four digits and you need to say it out loud long before you need the counting rules that build it.

words.note: Forbidden — a passive participle used as an adjective. On a sign it comes FIRST, before the thing forbidden.
Smoking — a maṣdar, the verbal noun of L3-M1. t is a sun letter: at-tadkhīn. Signs almost always carry the article.

sentences.trap: English signs say "no smoking" with a negative word. Arabic says "forbidden, the smoking" with an adjective and a noun, in that order — and the noun keeps its al-.
sentences.sound: mam-NOOʿ at-tad-KHEEN — the ʿ at the end of mamnūʿ is a squeeze in the throat, not a silent letter.

variations.cue: Smoking is forbidden in the restaurant
variations.changed: where: hunā → fī al-maṭʿam
the order — a sentence rather than a sign, and both are correct

mistake.why: The English sign translated word for word. lā negates verbs, not notices. A notice is mamnūʿ at-tadkhīn.

sentences.usage: Read off a wall in every airport, restaurant and lift in the Arab world — the single most useful sign to decode.

words.note: The paper form you fill in. Feminine, so everything beside it takes -a: hādhihi al-istimāra maṭlūba.
Required — the same participle shape as mamnūʿ. It agrees: maṭlūba beside a feminine noun, maṭlūb beside a masculine one.

sentences.trap: "Required" never changes in English. Here it must agree twice over — with the form's gender, and with nothing else in the sentence.
sentences.sound: HAA-dhi-hi lis-ti-MAA-ra maṭ-LOO-ba — the ṭ is the heavy t, said with the tongue flat.

variations.cue: The date is required on the receipt
variations.changed: what is required — masculine, so maṭlūb loses its -a
the day dropped, for a counter conversation

mistake.why: istimāra is feminine, so both the pointer and the participle move: hādhihi al-istimāra maṭlūba. Two agreements, one noun.

sentences.usage: What the clerk says when they hand you a sheet, and what you repeat back to be sure.
sentences.mnemonic: The paper is feminine, so everything around it grows an -a.

sentences.cue: I have to pay the rent

words.note: I pay. Same shape as L2's adhhab and adrus, and it follows yajibu an the same way. dafaʿtu is the past, I paid.
Rent — the money, not the act. The initial ī is long: EE-jaar. Moon letter, so the article stays al-.

sentences.trap: yajibu an is L3-M2's frame and money does not change it. The only new thing here is the verb between them.

variations.cue: I have to pay from my account
variations.changed: what is paid → where it is paid from

variations.cue: I have to pay the bill today
variations.changed: what: al-ījār → al-fātūra

mistake.why: The an is not optional after yajibu. It is the joint the sentence turns on: yajibu an adfaʿ al-ījār.

sentences.usage: The sentence in your head on the first of the month, and the one you say when declining an invitation.

sentences.cue: Where do I pay the bill?

words.note: Bill or invoice. Feminine. Its plural fawātīr is a broken plural — take it as a second word, not as a rule.

sentences.trap: English needs "do" to ask this. Arabic needs nothing at all: ayna and then the plain verb, in the order they come.

variations.cue: Where do I pay the rent?
variations.changed: what: al-fātūra → al-ījār
the verb dropped — ayna alone is enough for a place

mistake.why: The a- of adfaʿ is already "I". Adding anā is the English habit and turns a question into an oddly emphatic one.

sentences.usage: The first sentence in any office where the queue is not signposted.
sentences.mnemonic: ayna plus the verb. No do, no anā.

sentences.display: min faḍlika, hal yumkinu an tusāʿidanī
sentences.script: من فضلك، هل يمكن أن تساعدني
sentences.literal: From your-favour, question it-is-possible that you-help-me

words.note: Office or desk — the counter you are standing at when you say this. Broken plural makātib, taken as vocabulary.

sentences.trap: Every piece of this is already yours: min faḍlika from L1-M8, hal from L1-M2, yumkinu an from L3-M2, tusāʿidanī from L2. The module opens no new politeness — it only puts the old ones at a counter.
sentences.sound: min FAḌ-li-ka, hal YUM-ki-nu an tu-SAA-ʿi-da-nee — a real pause at the comma.

variations.display: law samaḥta, hal yumkinu an tusāʿidanī
variations.script: لو سمحت، هل يمكن أن تساعدني
variations.cue: Excuse me, can you help me?
variations.changed: the opener: min faḍlika → L2-M1's law samaḥta

variations.display: min faḍliki, hal yumkinu an tusāʿidanī
variations.script: من فضلك، هل يمكن أن تساعدني
variations.changed: who you are asking: faḍlika → faḍliki

mistake.why: Not wrong, but bare. At a counter the yumkinu an is what makes it a request instead of an interrogation: hal yumkinu an tusāʿidanī.

sentences.usage: The opening line at any desk — bank, town hall, pharmacy, letting agent.

words.note: Open — the participle again, and an adjective in every way that matters. maftūḥa beside a feminine noun.

sentences.trap: maftūḥ describes a state, not an action. It never means "opens" or "is opening" — for that you would need the verb, which is L4's.
sentences.sound: al-MAK-tab maf-TOOḤ al-AAN — the final ḥ is breathed out, not swallowed.

variations.changed: what is open — feminine, so maftūḥa
which participle: L2-M7's mawjūd, the same shape all along

mistake.why: maktab is masculine, so it takes maftūḥ with no -a. The participle agrees exactly as any adjective does.

sentences.usage: Read off a door, or asked on the phone before you set out.
sentences.mnemonic: Open is a state, and states agree.

sentences.cue: The bank is closed on Friday

words.note: Bank — a borrowed word, said as it looks. b is a moon letter: al-bank.
Closed, the opposite number of maftūḥ and the same participle shape. mughlaqa beside a feminine noun.

sentences.trap: yawm al-jumʿa is an iḍāfa — L3-M2's two nouns touching, "the day of the Friday". No preposition is needed where English wants "on".
sentences.sound: al-BANK MUGH-laq YAWM al-JUM-ʿa — the gh is a gargle, like a French r.

variations.changed: what, and when

variations.cue: The pharmacy is closed on Friday
variations.changed: what is closed — feminine, so mughlaqa

mistake.why: The fī is the English "on" carried across. yawm al-jumʿa already means "on Friday" by itself.

sentences.usage: The single most useful fact about a working week you did not grow up in.
sentences.mnemonic: Closed on the day of the Friday — no preposition anywhere.

sentences.cue: The rent is a thousand riyals a month

words.note: A thousand. alfayn is two thousand, the dual again. Vocabulary, not a counting system — that is L4's.
Month. sh is a sun letter: ash-shahr. fī ash-shahr is "a month" in the sense of per month.
The amount — the number written on the form. What a clerk asks for when they will not say "money".
Money in general, the substance. For a specific sum on a form, use mablagh instead.

sentences.trap: There is no verb here at all. Arabic states a price the way it states any equation — the thing, then what it is — and the copula stays absent as it has since L1-M1.

variations.changed: the price → the demand for it

variations.cue: I have money in the bank
variations.changed: a price → what you hold, with L1-M7's ʿindī

mistake.why: The huwa is an English "is" smuggled in. Arabic joins the two halves with nothing: al-ījār alf riyāl.

sentences.usage: Said and heard at every letting agent, and the shape of every price you will be quoted.
sentences.mnemonic: No verb, no "is", just the two facts touching.

sentences.cue: A signature is required on this form

words.note: Signature. t is a sun letter: at-tawqīʿ. Masculine, so the participle beside it is maṭlūb with no -a.
Sign — the command, said to you across a counter. waqqiʿī to a woman, exactly as khudh became khudhī.
Date — the one on the form, and also "history". The ʾ is a hamza: ta-ʾ-REEKH, with a catch.

sentences.trap: Two participles a metre apart on the same desk, agreeing differently: at-tawqīʿ maṭlūb (masculine) but al-istimāra maṭlūba (feminine). Read the ending, not the English.

variations.changed: the notice → the instruction you are given
where it is required → when

mistake.why: The -a has drifted onto the wrong word. maṭlūb agrees with at-tawqīʿ, the signature, not with the form it sits on.

sentences.usage: The line on the form itself, and the one the clerk taps with a pen.
sentences.mnemonic: The participle looks left, at its own noun.

sentences.cue: Take the receipt from the clerk

words.note: Receipt — the slip you keep. Same root as L2-M10's waṣaltu, arrive: what arrives in your hand.
My account — L2-M5's ḥisāb with the -ī of raʾsī and ismī, its first outing on this ladder. Tap ḥisāb for the plain word.

sentences.trap: Never leave a counter without the waṣl. Grammatically it is an ordinary object; practically it is the only proof the mablagh was paid.

variations.cue: Take the receipt from the clerk
variations.changed: who is told, and who hands it over — both feminine
who it comes from → a softening min faḍlika

mistake.why: ilā is towards; min is from. Reversed, this tells the clerk to take the receipt off you, which is the opposite of what you want.

sentences.usage: The last sentence of every transaction, and the one worth saying to yourself before you walk away.
sentences.mnemonic: min brings it to you; ilā takes it away.
